paragraphs.heading: Rock born from melt
paragraphs.text: Igneous rock, also called magmatic rock, belongs to the three main rock types, together with sedimentary and metamorphic rock. The name comes from the Latin igneus, meaning fiery. It forms when magma or lava cools and solidifies. Magma is molten rock, which typically carries suspended crystals and dissolved gases; once it reaches the surface it is called lava. The magma can come from partial melts of existing rocks in the mantle or crust of a terrestrial planet. The melting typically has one or more of three causes: a rise in temperature, a drop in pressure, or a change in composition.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is found
paragraphs.text: Igneous rock makes up most of the Earth's oceanic crust. It also forms about 15% of the Earth's current land surface. By volume, 90–95% of the top 16 kilometres of the Earth's crust is igneous and metamorphic rock taken together. In some special circumstances igneous rocks host important mineral deposits, known as ores. Granites and diorites are commonly associated with tungsten, tin and uranium, and gabbros with ores of chromium and platinum.

paragraphs.heading: Cooling underground
paragraphs.text: Igneous rocks are either intrusive or extrusive. Intrusive rocks, which are the majority, form when magma cools and turns solid inside a planet's crust. A body of intrusive rock is called an intrusion, and the pre-existing rock around it is called country rock. Because country rock is an excellent insulator of heat, the magma takes a long time to cool, and intrusive rocks come out coarse-grained. Their mineral grains can generally be picked out with the naked eye. Granite, gabbro and diorite are common intrusive rocks.

paragraphs.heading: Deep and shallow intrusions
paragraphs.text: The central cores of major mountain ranges are made of intrusive igneous rock. These cores are called batholiths, and when erosion exposes them they may occupy huge areas of the Earth's surface. Intrusive rocks that form at depth in the crust are termed plutonic and are usually coarse-grained. Those formed near the surface are called subvolcanic or hypabyssal rocks. They are usually much finer-grained and often look like volcanic rock.

paragraphs.heading: Cooling at the surface
paragraphs.text: Extrusive igneous rock, also known as volcanic rock, forms when molten magma cools on the Earth's surface. The magma arrives through fissures or volcanic eruptions and solidifies rapidly. That is why such rocks are fine-grained or even glassy. The most common extrusive igneous rock is basalt, which forms lava flows, lava sheets and lava plateaus. Some kinds of basalt solidify into long polygonal columns, as at the Giant's Causeway in Antrim, Northern Ireland.

paragraphs.heading: Runny lava and sticky lava
paragraphs.text: How lava behaves depends on its viscosity, which is set by temperature, composition and crystal content. High-temperature magma, most of it basaltic in composition, behaves much like thick oil and, as it cools, like treacle. Felsic magma, such as rhyolite, usually erupts at a low temperature. Its viscosity can reach 10,000 times that of basalt. Volcanoes with rhyolitic magma commonly erupt explosively. When felsic and intermediate magmas erupt, it is often violent, and the explosions are driven by dissolved gases being released, typically water vapour but also carbon dioxide.

paragraphs.heading: What eruptions leave behind
paragraphs.text: Explosively erupted pyroclastic material is called tephra, and it includes tuff, agglomerate and ignimbrite. Fine volcanic ash is erupted too, and it forms ash tuff deposits that can often cover vast areas. Because volcanic rocks are mostly fine-grained or glassy, telling the different types of extrusive igneous rock apart is much harder than telling the intrusive types apart.
